shared.title: Make the Call: Technology & AI in Grade 6
shared.bigQuestion: When does technology strengthen our learning—and what choices keep the thinking, safety, and responsibility with us?
shared.summary: During the Grade 6 rotations, students work through fast, concrete technology and AI decisions. In pairs and table groups they test whether authorship can be guessed from style, sort six classroom situations, repair a shortcut prompt, challenge a confident AI response, and propose a usable class commitment. Each student then writes and signs a one-page learning, technology, and AI agreement for the teacher who will receive them.

learningArc.label: Launch
learningArc.studentAction: Name one learning job a tool can help with and one choice that could weaken trust.
learningArc.outcome: Technology is discussed through learning purposes and responsible decisions, not app popularity.

learningArc.label: Detect
learningArc.studentAction: Vote HUMAN, AI, or CANNOT TELL for three samples, then point to evidence and its limits.
learningArc.outcome: Students replace style-based guesses with questions about process, sources, drafts, and explanation.

learningArc.label: Sort
learningArc.studentAction: Place classroom situations in HELPS LEARNING, CHECK IT, or STOP + ASK and defend the call.
learningArc.outcome: Students reason with privacy, accuracy, ownership, attribution, and learning purpose.

learningArc.label: Prompt
learningArc.studentAction: Repair a prompt so AI questions and coaches instead of completing the work.
learningArc.outcome: The learner's decisions, evidence, and final explanation remain visible.

learningArc.label: Repair
learningArc.studentAction: Mark a confident AI response KEEP, CHECK, or CHANGE and rewrite one weak claim.
learningArc.outcome: Students separate useful language from reliable evidence.

learningArc.label: Draft
learningArc.studentAction: Write and stress-test one table commitment using a real scenario.
learningArc.outcome: The class gathers observable commitments rather than broad slogans.

learningArc.label: Agree
learningArc.studentAction: Complete a personal learning, technology, and AI agreement.
learningArc.outcome: Each student names a support, a commitment, a stop-and-ask moment, and a teacher question.

learningArc.label: Sign
learningArc.studentAction: Check, sign, and place the named page in the rotation collection tray.
learningArc.outcome: The receiving teacher gets a practical starting point for a follow-up conversation.

student.label: STUDENT PATH
student.title: Make the Call: Technology & AI in Grade 6
student.why: You will use technology, search, and sometimes AI during Grade 6. This lab helps you know what to check, what to keep as your own thinking, what information to protect, and when to ask for help.
student.summary: Work with a partner and table to investigate realistic classroom choices. You will make evidence-based calls, improve a prompt and an AI response, help write a class commitment, and finish with an agreement in your own words.
student.grouping: Partner talk and tables of 3–4 for the investigations; your personal agreement is individual because it describes your commitments, supports, and question.
bring: A pencil or another way to record your ideas
Your reasons, questions, and willingness to change your mind
No passwords, account names, photos, schedules, or private family information
student.firstMove: Think of one time technology helped you imagine, practise, organize, check, communicate, create, access support, or collaborate. Tell a partner what it helped you do.

quickReference.firstMove: Tell a partner about one time technology helped you learn. Name what it helped you do.
quickReference.handIn: Put your named agreement in the rotation tray. It is practice, not a grade.
quickReference.missed: Ask for the short scenario and agreement. Use the four-question check if you get stuck.

student.firstMoveNote: Name the learning job, not just the app or device. Then predict one choice that could make the result less useful or trustworthy.
steps: Detect: vote HUMAN, AI, or CANNOT TELL and explain what your clue can prove.
Sort: place classroom situations in HELPS LEARNING, CHECK IT, or STOP + ASK.
Prompt: turn ‘do it for us’ into a prompt that asks questions and waits for student decisions.
Repair: mark a confident AI response KEEP, CHECK, or CHANGE and rewrite one problem.
Draft: help your table write one commitment that tells people what to do in a real moment.
Agree: choose two class commitments and write one commitment of your own.
Personalize: name one support that helps you learn, one stop-and-ask moment, and one teacher question.
Sign and submit: check that the agreement sounds like you and contains no private account information.
choices: Use speaking, writing, pointing, table cards, dictation to an adult, or labelled drawings to show your reasoning.
Disagree with a table call when you can give a reason tied to learning, privacy, accuracy, ownership, or fairness.
Describe a school-learning support that is useful to your teacher; private medical, diagnostic, or family details are not required.
student.product: One table commitment plus your signed, one-page My Grade 6 Learning, Technology & AI Agreement.
student.finish: You can explain one decision your thinking group made, show how a prompt or response was improved, and submit an agreement with a specific commitment, a stop-and-ask moment, a learning support, and a teacher question.
student.handInOrSave: Place the named agreement in the labelled rotation tray. It goes privately to your receiving Grade 6 teacher as the start of a conversation; it is not graded.
student.ifAbsentOrStuck: If absent, ask for the short scenario-and-agreement route. If stuck, choose one situation and use four questions: What is the learning purpose? Is private information involved? What needs checking? Who makes the final decision?
student.spacesNote: The named agreement is not posted to SpacesEDU. Later in September, you may choose stronger evidence for a Learning Story about how your thinking changed.

family.label: FAMILY WINDOW
family.title: The first Grade 6 technology decisions
family.summary: During the opening rotations, students spend one 60-minute lesson investigating realistic choices about search, devices, and AI. The focus is practical: privacy, checking claims, keeping student thinking visible, explaining help received, and knowing when to stop and ask an adult.
family.whyThisMatters: Students need more than a slogan such as ‘use AI responsibly.’ They practise making and defending a decision in situations they may actually encounter, including a confident claim with no source, a request for private information, and a tool that offers to complete the student's work.
family.whatStudentsDo: Students first work in pairs and tables to examine three authorship samples, sort six scenarios, repair a shortcut prompt, audit four claims in an AI response, and write one testable table commitment. In the final ten minutes, each student completes and signs an individual learning, technology, and AI agreement.

quickReference.atSchool: In pairs and table groups, students sort six realistic situations, improve an AI prompt and response, then write their own one-page agreement.
quickReference.home: Nothing to prepare or finish at home.
quickReference.assessment: The teacher observes reasoning and revision. The agreement is practice—not a grade or placement decision.
quickReference.spaces: The agreement stays with the teacher. Selected learning and feedback may appear in SpacesEDU later.

family.product: A table contributes one proposed class commitment. Each student submits a one-page agreement naming a useful learning purpose, two class commitments, one personal commitment, a stop-and-ask situation, a learning support, and a question for the receiving teacher.
family.assessment: This is low-stakes formative evidence. The teacher listens for clear reasons, willingness to verify, respect for privacy and authentic voices, honest explanation of tool help, and the student's ability to keep final decisions visible. The agreement is not graded and does not affect class placement.
family.agreementNote: This is a student-to-teacher learning agreement, not a legal contract or family consent form. It does not give permission to create accounts or use unapproved tools, and it does not replace Surrey Schools policies or teacher directions. Commitments may be discussed and revised as the class learns.
family.groupAndIndividualEvidence: Table talk shows how students compare evidence, share airtime, and revise a decision. The individual page preserves each student's own commitment, support, and question. Named completed agreements stay private with the teacher.

shared.title: Source Lab & Newsroom
shared.bigQuestion: What does this source show—and what would we need to check before believing more?
shared.summary: Begin with one real photograph, map, graph, quotation, headline, short text, or video. Students examine it together before they receive an explanation, make a claim, or decide what to investigate next.
shared.cadence: Use a Quick Look for an 8–12 minute source conversation or a Deep Dive when the source deserves comparison, research, or a longer response.
shared.sourcePromise: Every source is visible, named, dated when possible, and linked to its publisher or archive. Current sources receive a review date; historical sources keep their archive credit and context.

routes.label: QUICK LOOK
routes.use: One source, one careful claim, one uncertainty. End with discussion or save one question.

routes.label: DEEP DIVE
routes.path: Look → Notice → Claim → Compare → Check → Next
routes.use: Open the source record, compare another source or perspective, and create a response only when the question earns more time.

routine.label: LOOK
routine.title: Meet the source
routine.prompt: Study it quietly once. What is literally here before anyone explains it?

routine.label: NOTICE
routine.title: Collect clues
routine.prompt: Point to exact words, dates, numbers, labels, objects, sounds, or visible details.

routine.label: CLAIM
routine.title: Make a careful first idea
routine.prompt: What might the source show or suggest? What question or uncertainty must stay attached?

routine.label: COMPARE
routine.title: Test the idea with other people
routine.prompt: In a pair or team, compare interpretations. Which clues support each idea, and where are we relying on assumptions?

routine.label: CHECK
routine.title: Open the source record
routine.prompt: Who made it, when, for what purpose, and what changes after reading its caption, context, data notes, or another source?

routine.label: NEXT
routine.title: Choose how this source ends
routine.prompt: Revise the claim, stop after a useful discussion, save a strong question, or continue into research, writing, data, art, design, or action.

endings.label: DISCUSS & STOP
endings.title: A useful conversation can be enough
endings.detail: Name one careful conclusion and one uncertainty. Nothing needs to be posted.

endings.label: SAVE A SEED
endings.title: Carry one question forward
endings.detail: Write a promising question in an inquiry notebook, team passport, or the class question wall.

endings.label: FOLLOW IT
endings.title: Continue when the question earns more time
endings.detail: The teacher may choose a source set, field observation, interview, data task, story, model, or design challenge.

student.title: Start with the source—not the answer.
student.summary: Your job is to collect clues, make a possible claim, hear another interpretation, and revise when the caption, context, or another source changes the evidence.
student.firstMove: Look quietly. Point to one exact detail and say, “I notice ___.” Do not explain it yet.

inquiryRoutes.title: Talk it through
inquiryRoutes.detail: The class makes sense of the story and stops. Good thinking does not need to become an assignment.

inquiryRoutes.title: Keep the question
inquiryRoutes.detail: Write one inquiry seed you genuinely want to revisit. Include why it matters and what kind of evidence could help.

inquiryRoutes.title: Build, teach, or act
inquiryRoutes.detail: When a question connects to our Big Ideas, the class may investigate, make something, teach an audience, or propose a careful solution.

student.finish: I can say what the source supports, what remains uncertain, and the next question I would ask.
student.absentOrStuck: Ask a partner for the source, the class question, and one detail they can point to. Add your own question before asking for the class conclusion.
student.spacesNote: Most Source Lab work stays in discussion, notebooks, and class work. Only selected evidence or reflection belongs in SpacesEDU.

family.title: What families should know about Source Lab & Newsroom
family.summary: Students regularly examine a real current or historical source and practise separating observation, inference, evidence, context, and uncertainty. Some sources lead only to a short conversation; others connect to a larger inquiry or project.

quickReference.label: What students do
quickReference.detail: Study one visible, teacher-reviewed source, identify exact clues, compare interpretations, open its context, and decide whether a question deserves more investigation.

quickReference.label: How collaboration works
quickReference.detail: Pairs or small groups are common because explaining, questioning, and revising with other people strengthens the thinking. Individual reflection is used when each student's own learning matters.

quickReference.label: Visual clue challenges
quickReference.detail: The teacher leads one whole-class visual challenge while teams record three precise details, a place or time range, one uncertainty, and a revision after the reveal. Students do not need an account and do not post a public response.

quickReference.label: How it is assessed
quickReference.detail: The teacher looks for careful use of evidence, useful questions, listening, revision, and honest uncertainty. A student's political opinion is not graded.

quickReference.label: What comes home
quickReference.detail: You may see a discussion question, inquiry seed, or selected learning artifact. Most stories remain short classroom conversations and do not become portfolio posts.

conversationPrompts: What detail changed or complicated your first idea?
Whose experience or perspective was missing from the source?
What would you need to check before sharing that claim?

shared.title: Make the Call: Technology & AI in Grade 6
shared.bigQuestion: When does technology strengthen our learning—and what choices keep the thinking, safety, and responsibility with us?
shared.summary: During the Grade 6 rotations, students work through fast, concrete technology and AI decisions. In pairs and table groups they test whether authorship can be guessed from style, sort six classroom situations, repair a shortcut prompt, challenge a confident AI response, and propose a usable class commitment. Each student then writes and signs a one-page learning, technology, and AI agreement for the teacher who will receive them.

learningArc.label: Launch
learningArc.studentAction: Name one learning job a tool can help with and one choice that could weaken trust.
learningArc.outcome: Technology is discussed through learning purposes and responsible decisions, not app popularity.

learningArc.label: Detect
learningArc.studentAction: Vote HUMAN, AI, or CANNOT TELL for three samples, then point to evidence and its limits.
learningArc.outcome: Students replace style-based guesses with questions about process, sources, drafts, and explanation.

learningArc.label: Sort
learningArc.studentAction: Place classroom situations in HELPS LEARNING, CHECK IT, or STOP + ASK and defend the call.
learningArc.outcome: Students reason with privacy, accuracy, ownership, attribution, and learning purpose.

learningArc.label: Prompt
learningArc.studentAction: Repair a prompt so AI questions and coaches instead of completing the work.
learningArc.outcome: The learner's decisions, evidence, and final explanation remain visible.

learningArc.label: Repair
learningArc.studentAction: Mark a confident AI response KEEP, CHECK, or CHANGE and rewrite one weak claim.
learningArc.outcome: Students separate useful language from reliable evidence.

learningArc.label: Draft
learningArc.studentAction: Write and stress-test one table commitment using a real scenario.
learningArc.outcome: The class gathers observable commitments rather than broad slogans.

learningArc.label: Agree
learningArc.studentAction: Complete a personal learning, technology, and AI agreement.
learningArc.outcome: Each student names a support, a commitment, a stop-and-ask moment, and a teacher question.

learningArc.label: Sign
learningArc.studentAction: Check, sign, and place the named page in the rotation collection tray.
learningArc.outcome: The receiving teacher gets a practical starting point for a follow-up conversation.

student.label: STUDENT PATH
student.title: Make the Call: Technology & AI in Grade 6
student.why: You will use technology, search, and sometimes AI during Grade 6. This lab helps you know what to check, what to keep as your own thinking, what information to protect, and when to ask for help.
student.summary: Work with a partner and table to investigate realistic classroom choices. You will make evidence-based calls, improve a prompt and an AI response, help write a class commitment, and finish with an agreement in your own words.
student.grouping: Partner talk and tables of 3–4 for the investigations; your personal agreement is individual because it describes your commitments, supports, and question.
bring: A pencil or another way to record your ideas
Your reasons, questions, and willingness to change your mind
No passwords, account names, photos, schedules, or private family information
student.firstMove: Think of one time technology helped you imagine, practise, organize, check, communicate, create, access support, or collaborate. Tell a partner what it helped you do.

quickReference.firstMove: Tell a partner about one time technology helped you learn. Name what it helped you do.
quickReference.handIn: Put your named agreement in the rotation tray. It is practice, not a grade.
quickReference.missed: Ask for the short scenario and agreement. Use the four-question check if you get stuck.

student.firstMoveNote: Name the learning job, not just the app or device. Then predict one choice that could make the result less useful or trustworthy.
steps: Detect: vote HUMAN, AI, or CANNOT TELL and explain what your clue can prove.
Sort: place classroom situations in HELPS LEARNING, CHECK IT, or STOP + ASK.
Prompt: turn ‘do it for us’ into a prompt that asks questions and waits for student decisions.
Repair: mark a confident AI response KEEP, CHECK, or CHANGE and rewrite one problem.
Draft: help your table write one commitment that tells people what to do in a real moment.
Agree: choose two class commitments and write one commitment of your own.
Personalize: name one support that helps you learn, one stop-and-ask moment, and one teacher question.
Sign and submit: check that the agreement sounds like you and contains no private account information.
choices: Use speaking, writing, pointing, table cards, dictation to an adult, or labelled drawings to show your reasoning.
Disagree with a table call when you can give a reason tied to learning, privacy, accuracy, ownership, or fairness.
Describe a school-learning support that is useful to your teacher; private medical, diagnostic, or family details are not required.
student.product: One table commitment plus your signed, one-page My Grade 6 Learning, Technology & AI Agreement.
student.finish: You can explain one decision your thinking group made, show how a prompt or response was improved, and submit an agreement with a specific commitment, a stop-and-ask moment, a learning support, and a teacher question.
student.handInOrSave: Place the named agreement in the labelled rotation tray. It goes privately to your receiving Grade 6 teacher as the start of a conversation; it is not graded.
student.ifAbsentOrStuck: If absent, ask for the short scenario-and-agreement route. If stuck, choose one situation and use four questions: What is the learning purpose? Is private information involved? What needs checking? Who makes the final decision?
student.spacesNote: The named agreement is not posted to SpacesEDU. Later in September, you may choose stronger evidence for a Learning Story about how your thinking changed.

family.label: FAMILY WINDOW
family.title: The first Grade 6 technology decisions
family.summary: During the opening rotations, students spend one 60-minute lesson investigating realistic choices about search, devices, and AI. The focus is practical: privacy, checking claims, keeping student thinking visible, explaining help received, and knowing when to stop and ask an adult.
family.whyThisMatters: Students need more than a slogan such as ‘use AI responsibly.’ They practise making and defending a decision in situations they may actually encounter, including a confident claim with no source, a request for private information, and a tool that offers to complete the student's work.
family.whatStudentsDo: Students first work in pairs and tables to examine three authorship samples, sort six scenarios, repair a shortcut prompt, audit four claims in an AI response, and write one testable table commitment. In the final ten minutes, each student completes and signs an individual learning, technology, and AI agreement.

quickReference.atSchool: In pairs and table groups, students sort six realistic situations, improve an AI prompt and response, then write their own one-page agreement.
quickReference.home: Nothing to prepare or finish at home.
quickReference.assessment: The teacher observes reasoning and revision. The agreement is practice—not a grade or placement decision.
quickReference.spaces: The agreement stays with the teacher. Selected learning and feedback may appear in SpacesEDU later.

family.product: A table contributes one proposed class commitment. Each student submits a one-page agreement naming a useful learning purpose, two class commitments, one personal commitment, a stop-and-ask situation, a learning support, and a question for the receiving teacher.
family.assessment: This is low-stakes formative evidence. The teacher listens for clear reasons, willingness to verify, respect for privacy and authentic voices, honest explanation of tool help, and the student's ability to keep final decisions visible. The agreement is not graded and does not affect class placement.
family.agreementNote: This is a student-to-teacher learning agreement, not a legal contract or family consent form. It does not give permission to create accounts or use unapproved tools, and it does not replace Surrey Schools policies or teacher directions. Commitments may be discussed and revised as the class learns.
family.groupAndIndividualEvidence: Table talk shows how students compare evidence, share airtime, and revise a decision. The individual page preserves each student's own commitment, support, and question. Named completed agreements stay private with the teacher.

shared.title: Five ways to become known
shared.bigQuestion: What can we learn about ourselves, one another, and this place without asking anyone to share a private story?
shared.summary: Across five connected days, students tell a low-risk object story, show how they reason with number size, name useful learning conditions, gather exact observations from the school grounds, and choose one specific example for a Friday Learning Story.

learningArc.label: Story
learningArc.studentAction: Choose an ordinary object, point to five visible clues, tell a three-beat story, and improve it after one listener question.
learningArc.outcome: The class begins with voice, listening, visible evidence, and a safe fictional route.

learningArc.label: Number
learningArc.studentAction: Place very large and very small quantities on accurate scales and explain one surprising position.
learningArc.outcome: The teacher sees strategies and misconceptions without reducing students to a score.

learningArc.label: Learning
learningArc.studentAction: Test which conditions help in real classroom situations and write one useful request or strategy.
learningArc.outcome: Students describe changeable supports and actions rather than fixed learning labels.

learningArc.label: Place
learningArc.studentAction: Collect exact sound, movement, colour, light, and texture evidence outside or from an equivalent observation station.
learningArc.outcome: Observation stays separate from inference, and the class gathers material for a place response.

learningArc.label: Synthesize
learningArc.studentAction: Choose one specific example, name what it shows, set one realistic goal, and revise for a teacher or family audience.
learningArc.outcome: One meaningful Learning Story replaces several small uploads.

family.agreementNote: Students may use fictional, observation-only, written, spoken, visual, or recorded routes. Private family, medical, diagnostic, or painful information is not required.

shared.title: Who decides—and what does this place teach us?
shared.bigQuestion: How can maps, sources, local voices, and public decisions change what we understand about Surrey?
shared.summary: Students use the existing place, map, evidence, perspective, and government lessons as a live Surrey case. They distinguish observation from inference, learn from attributed local-Nation and district sources, sort who controls which decisions, and begin checking election claims after the official candidate list is available.

learningArc.label: Who decides?
learningArc.studentAction: Sort school, district, city, provincial, and federal decisions; explain the exact authority involved.
learningArc.outcome: Students distinguish influence, administration, voting, oversight, and final authority.

learningArc.studentAction: Gather local observations and compare what different maps and attributed sources make visible or leave out.
learningArc.outcome: Place learning remains specific to source, Nation, speaker, purpose, and protocol.

learningArc.label: Check a campaign claim
learningArc.studentAction: Label fact, opinion, claim, or promise; trace one checkable part to an official or independent source.
learningArc.outcome: A campaign statement becomes evidence to investigate, not a position students are told to support.

learningArc.label: Make meaning
learningArc.studentAction: Build a concise place-and-decision display with exact source credit, one careful claim, one missing perspective, and one next question.
learningArc.outcome: The display makes local learning visible without turning a generic craft into reconciliation.

learningArc.label: Carry it forward
learningArc.studentAction: Choose one election, place, or power question worth following in the October Newsroom.
learningArc.outcome: Strong questions continue; no extra SpacesEDU post is required.

student.label: STUDENT PATH
student.title: Check the promise before the vote
student.why: Candidates use facts, opinions, claims, and promises to persuade voters. You can check the source, the office's real power, and the trade-offs before making up your own mind.
student.summary: Work with a partner and team to trace one claim, compare statements with the same questions, take part in a civic hearing, and prepare for a private Student Vote ballot.
student.grouping: Pairs and teams for investigation; whole class for the hearing; a private individual ballot
bring: One source detail you can point to
A question that does not assume the answer
Respect for other people's private choices
student.firstMove: Read one short campaign statement. Underline the exact promise. Circle what could be checked. Put a question mark beside anything the office may not control alone.

quickReference.firstMove: Underline the promise, circle the checkable part, and question the office's authority.
quickReference.handIn: Keep the pair claim trail and team comparison board in class. Your ballot choice stays private.
quickReference.missed: Open one dated statement and its original source. Add the office, one checkable claim, and one honest uncertainty.

student.firstMoveNote: A strong promise can still require a council or board vote, money, another level of government, public input, or time.
steps: Identify: Who said it, when, and which office are they seeking?
Label: Is it a fact, opinion, claim, or promise?
Trace: Open the original source for the strongest checkable part.
Match: Can this office decide it alone, act with others, influence it, or not control it?
Compare: Use the same headings for every candidate statement.
Question: Ask about evidence, cost, trade-offs, missing perspectives, or what happens next.
Decide privately: Use the Student Vote ballot only after you understand the offices and evidence.
choices: Use a teacher-read excerpt, projected source, short text, audio, or paper source card with the same credit and context.
Contribute by pointing, sorting, speaking, writing, drawing a decision path, or asking a question.
Change your mind, remain uncertain, or keep your ballot choice private; your political preference is not assessed.
student.product: One pair claim trail, one team comparison board, and a short reflection on the evidence or process—not on which name you chose.
student.finish: You can check a campaign statement, explain what the office can and cannot do alone, compare choices fairly, and protect ballot privacy.
student.handInOrSave: Keep investigation notes and the comparison board in class. Follow the class Student Vote routine; never put your ballot choice in SpacesEDU.
student.ifAbsentOrStuck: Start with one statement and four questions: Who said it? What is promised? What evidence checks it? Who has the power to act?
student.spacesNote: No extra SpacesEDU post is planned. Your ballot choice remains private.

shared.eyebrow: OCTOBER · RESULTS AND WHAT HAPPENS NEXT
shared.title: Election day to next steps: what happens now?
shared.bigQuestion: What do election results tell us—and what still has to happen before a promise becomes a public decision?
shared.summary: Students use the Newsroom to read official Surrey results and CIVIX Student Vote results when each is released. They compare patterns carefully, follow one promise through the people, votes, budgets, approvals, and time it may require, and identify ways people can continue to influence public decisions after election day.

learningArc.label: Election day
learningArc.studentAction: Notice which Surrey offices are being elected and wait for official, dated results rather than reposting early claims or guesses.
learningArc.outcome: Students understand that result status and source matter.

learningArc.label: Read the results
learningArc.studentAction: Open the official Surrey results and record office, names, totals or shares, result status, source, and update time.
learningArc.outcome: The class builds an accurate result record for mayor, council, and school trustees.

learningArc.label: Compare carefully
learningArc.studentAction: Compare official and Student Vote results when both are available; describe a pattern without guessing why it happened.
learningArc.outcome: Students separate numerical patterns from unsupported explanations about voters.

learningArc.label: Follow a promise
learningArc.studentAction: Trace one promise through the council or board decision, staff work, budget, other approvals, public input, and time it may require.
learningArc.outcome: Winning an election is distinguished from having unlimited or immediate power.

learningArc.label: Keep participating
learningArc.studentAction: Choose one respectful next action a young person could take: follow a meeting, ask a question, write, verify, speak, create, volunteer, or revisit the evidence.
learningArc.outcome: Democratic participation continues between elections.

family.whatStudentsDo: Students verify the result source and status, compare official and Student Vote patterns without guessing at voters' motives, follow one earlier promise through a decision pathway, and identify ways participation continues after election day.
